## Why this doc exists

On 2026-07-25 two agents in different lanes each hit a multi-day silent outage,
within the same hour, in code that shares no call path: **pot-git publishing**
(su-a8ea9) and **hyperbee replication liveness** (su-e3b21). Neither was looking
for the other's bug. When one described its root cause in a coordination
message, the other recognised it immediately as the shape they had just fixed.

Comparing notes surfaced **two more the same day**, in two further lanes —
`restart_settle_barrier` (su-48ed7a) and the replication-liveness detector's
call site (su-055ae). **Four independent instances in one day, in four lanes,
found by four agents, none of whom was looking for this.** That is a pattern
worth a name, not four incident write-ups.

### The headline: it is the detectors, not the guards

The guard bugs (Shape A) are real, but they cost **hours**. What turned each of
them into a multi-**day** silent outage was that **every single instance was
paired with a detector that structurally could not see it** — Shape B or Shape C.
Four for four.

That is the claim worth acting on. A guard that wedges and *pages* is an
annoyance. A guard that wedges while every dashboard reads green is an outage
measured in days, and you find it by accident.

**If you change one thing after reading this, change a detector, not a latch.**

## Shape A — the absorbing-state guard

> **A guard whose baseline or latch advances only through its own success cannot
> clear itself. The first failure is permanent.**

This is an [absorbing state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absorbing_Markov_chain):
once entered, there is no transition out. It is easy to build by accident,
because the code reads as obviously correct — you advance the watermark *when
the thing succeeds*, which is exactly what you want, right up until the failure
path needs the watermark to move too.

### Instance 1 — the pot-git publish guards (three of them)

`own-head-publish.ts` judged the range `(priorSha, head]`, where `priorSha` is
the namespace ref — and the namespace ref is written **only after `guard.ok`**:

```ts
const guardBaseline = priorSha ?? input.genesisBaselineSha ?? null;
// …
if (!guard.ok) return { …, refused: guard };   // ← ref NOT written
await writeNamespaceRef(repoPath, …, headSha); // ← the only advance
```

So a refusal was terminal *by construction*: the baseline could only move
through the publish it was blocking, and every new commit made the refused range
bigger. One accidentally-committed 2.26 GB AppImage extraction on 2026-07-20 put
the range over the 500 MB cap; five days later the guard was still refusing, and
the measured total had grown from 2261 MB to 2415 MB. Deleting the files did
nothing — the guard enumerates objects introduced *anywhere* in the range.

The same shape, with three different baselines, in three guards:

| guard | baseline | advances on |
|---|---|---|
| `own_head_publish` | the namespace ref | its own successful publish |
| `ref_announce` | sigrefs | its own successful announce |
| GitHub egress | `origin/staging` | its own successful push |

Because the baselines are *different objects*, unwedging one by hand did not
unwedge the others — the manual namespace-ref re-base left `ref_announce` (which
reads sigrefs) refusing for hours afterwards. Full incident:
[p2p-publish-guard-total-over-cap-wedge](/internal/docs/agent-insights/p2p-publish-guard-total-over-cap-wedge).

### Instance 2 — the replication-liveness alarm latch

`replication-liveness.ts`'s `connected_never_replicated` latch
(`alarmedConnectedNever`) was cleared **only on an observed recovery**. On a
sustained-offline reset the window was cleared but the latch leaked — and since
the fire guard is `!st.alarmedConnectedNever`, a log that had alarmed and then
gone offline could never alarm again for the rest of the process lifetime, with
`deriveVerdict` reading a stale `no_replicator` off the dead latch.
(Found and fixed independently by su-e3b21; regression-tested in
`replication-liveness.test.ts`.)

### Where it hides: the reset path and the early exit

The publish-guard instances were on the obvious **refusal** path. The
replication instance was on the **reset** path — much harder to see, because the
success path *does* clear the latch and the code looks symmetric at a glance.

A third variant turned up in `origin-freshness-watchdog.ts` only because
su-e3b21 suggested checking reset paths. Its `of_alerted` latch is cleared in
exactly one place — the `verdict === 'ok'` branch — but an **earlier `continue`**
skipped the whole verdict block:

```ts
if (!existsSync(repoPath)) continue;   // ← bypasses the only clear
```

A pot that alarmed and then lost its bare store (host migration, or a repoKey
change like WI-5168's `slug` → `gh-<id>` move, which relocates that very path)
stranded the latch `true` forever and could never alarm again.

**So the checklist is not "does the failure path clear the state" but:**

- Does the **reset** path clear it, not just the recovery path?
- Does **every** early `continue` / `return` / `throw` before the clear leave it
  stranded?
- Can the state advance **at all** without the success it gates?

### The fix shape

Make progress possible without the blocked success:

- **Split the range.** Volume/aggregate refusals ("too much at once") are
  satisfiable by doing *less*, so publish the longest admissible prefix and let
  the backlog drain over ticks. The baseline moves; the wedge is self-clearing.
- **Attribute precisely.** A hard refusal (a real secret) should stop at the
  *exact* offending commit with everything before it shipped — never "somewhere
  in these 358 commits".
- **Budgets, not cliffs.** A scan cap that *blocks* when exceeded is absorbing;
  a scan cap that *stops and resumes next tick* is not.
- **Always ship an escape hatch that reaches every instance.** A runtime
  exemption existed for one of the three pot-git guards — and not for the one
  that was actually wedged.

## Shape B — self-report beats inference

> **When a component can report its own failure, the detector must consume that
> report. Inferring the same condition from a downstream proxy is strictly
> weaker, because the proxy can be confounded.**

Shape A is survivable *if something notices*. In both known instances, nothing
did — and that was a second, separate bug.

There **was** a purpose-built watchdog for the pot-git outage:
`origin-freshness-watchdog` (WI-5607), running the whole time, thresholds
`aheadCount >= 50` and `tipAge > 3h`, against an outage of **358 commits over 5
days**. It never fired — zero log lines in three days — because it measured
against the wrong branch:

```ts
const branch = entry.github_default_branch ?? 'main';   // ← the INGRESS branch
```

The bridge *egresses* to `staging`; `main` is the branch it ingests. And `main`
is fast-forwarded hourly by the **release pipeline** — a completely unrelated
mechanism — so both signals were structurally pinned healthy:

| signal | threshold | actual | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `aheadCount` | ≥ 50 | 24 | measured against `main`, kept fresh by the release pipeline |
| `originTipAgeMs` | > 3h | ~0 | `main` moved hourly, restarting the clock every sweep |

**A detector pointed at a signal kept fresh by an unrelated mechanism is
structurally blind.** It does not report a false negative — it reports
*correctly, about the wrong thing*, which is much harder to notice.

And the part that makes this a *rule* rather than a bug report: the publish leg
had been writing

```
metadata.own_head_publish.refused = 'total-over-cap'
```

on **every single tick** for five days, and logging it to the journal. The
system stated its own failure out loud, continuously, and no detector consumed
it. All that inference was unnecessary.

### The fix shape

- **Consume the self-report directly.** A sustained explicit refusal now alarms
  on its own.
- **Do not gate the self-report behind an inferred precondition.** The refusal
  check deliberately sits *before* the watchdog's `aheadCount <= 0` "nothing to
  push ⇒ definitionally healthy" early return — a refusal is true regardless of
  how any commit count comes out, and in this incident the commit count was the
  confounded signal.
- **Measure the thing you act on.** The watchdog now reads
  `github_bridge.egress_head` — what egress *actually landed* — not a mirror of
  a branch it never writes.

## Shape C — the detector that can only observe the healthy case

> **A detector whose coverage is gated on the success it exists to detect the
> absence of will report healthy precisely when the thing has failed.**

Shape A is about *state* that cannot advance. Shape B is about a detector
consuming a confounded *proxy* instead of a self-report. Shape C is about the
detector's **coverage**: it never runs at all on the failure case, so there is
no reading to be wrong.

This is the one that produces *zero* log lines and a green dashboard.

### Instance 4 — the replication-liveness detector's call site (WI-5781)

`sampleReplicationLiveness` has exactly **one** call site — `boot.ts:2400`,
**inside the merge pass's per-remote-log loop**. So the detector can only sample
logs it has **already attached**.

Read the code and it is entirely reasonable: *iterate the attached logs, sample
each one for liveness.* But the failure mode that matters is **a log that never
attached** — which is, by construction, not in the loop.

Both frames ran on the same host on the same build (run `20260725-153415`),
which makes the asymmetry the whole finding:

| | frame a (owner path) | frame b (member / join path) |
|---|---|---|
| swarm connections | live | live (14 `peer_connected` per harness) |
| received the peer's announce | yes | **yes** — `recv log=5fe26c2e0135` ×7 |
| peer log admitted | yes | **no** |
| detector lines emitted | 3 | **0** |
| detector fired + repaired | yes | — |

Frame b is not a false negative. **The detector never executed.**

**Why the member and not the owner.** The asymmetry is one line in
`classifySameHiveMember` (`boot.ts`):

```ts
if (memberDevices.includes(devicePubkey)) return 'admit';
return isOwner ? 'admit' : 'miss';   // member BUFFERS
```

On a membership miss the **owner admits** (a deliberate fix for a different
deadlock) and the **member buffers**. A buffered peer then retries every ~5s for
up to 30 minutes and is dropped with `announce_rejected` — never once producing
a liveness alarm. And it is *circular*: the member needs the owner's
`hive_members` row to admit the log, that row arrives via replication, and
replication requires the admission. `memberDevices` only ever advances on
success, so this is Shape A feeding Shape C.

#### Two traps when you confirm this from banked logs

Both nearly produced a wrong conclusion here.

1. **`recordBootEvent` writes to an in-memory ring** — not PG, not stdout. So
   `announce_admitted` / `announce_pending` greps return **zero hits on a
   PASSING run exactly as on a failing one**, and the restart you are
   investigating is the event that destroys the buffer. The absence reads as
   signal when it is an artifact. (Fixed: the sparse forensic kinds are now
   mirrored to stdout, so they land in the banked serve logs.)
2. **Do not compare runs of different length or scenario scope.** The failing
   run was a 5-minute `replication_soak`-only run; the runs it was first
   compared against were ~30-minute full-matrix runs with ~4× the activity.
   "Zero detector lines" looked damning until the durations were checked — it
   only survived scrutiny because three *other* runs emitted their first
   detector line ~45s after start, so 5 minutes was ample.

The general rule: before treating **silence** as evidence, prove the detector
would have spoken. Silence from a detector that never ran, a buffer that was
wiped, or a window too short to alarm are four different things that look
identical.

**The fix that landed (WI-5781).** Liveness is no longer driven only by the
admitted set. The merge pass now also samples `pendingPeers` — precisely "we
accepted this peer's announce, so we are *supposed* to be replicating it, and we
have not admitted it" — through a new `expected_never_admitted` axis with the
same durable-EI escalation as every other axis. That is the Shape C fix stated
concretely: *enumerate the expected set, alarm on the gap.* Note the expected
set was already in memory; no roster read or new I/O was needed, which is
typical — the expectation usually already exists somewhere, unread.

### Instance 3 — `restart_settle_barrier` (EI-18645423267952485)

The same shape one level up, at the harness layer. The barrier PASSes with
`order 80 didn't run this session` in **exactly** the case it exists to catch:
`restart_durability` had just run and **failed**. Its precondition ("did order
80 run?") was itself derived from the thing that failed, so absence-of-evidence
rendered as PASS. It masked a 25-minute outage.

### Why this is not Shape B

Shape B's fix is *"consume the self-report instead of inferring."* That does not
help here. **There is no self-report from a log that never attached** — nothing
instantiated a reporter for it. Absence does not announce itself.

The fix is different in kind:

- **Shape B:** the reporter exists; read it instead of guessing.
- **Shape C:** the reporter does not exist; you must enumerate the **expected**
  set and alarm on the difference from the **achieved** set.

### The fix shape

- **Enumerate expected, not achieved.** Iterate what *should* be attached /
  registered / running, and alarm on the gap. A loop over what succeeded can
  never see total failure.
- **Never derive a barrier's precondition from the thing it guards.** If "did X
  run?" is answered by X's own output, a failed X reads as "not applicable"
  rather than "failed".
- **Make absence loud.** `0 of N sampled` is a finding. A detector that emits
  nothing must be distinguishable from a detector that emits nothing *because
  everything is fine*.

## Shape D — the detector pointed at an empty set

Shapes A–C are all about a detector that *runs* over the right population and
still cannot see the failure. Shape D is nastier and simpler: the detector is
written correctly, enumerates exactly the right kind of thing, and is pointed at
a population that is **empty**. It then reports a clean pass forever.

This is distinct from checklist question 6. Question 6 asks whether you
enumerate the EXPECTED set or the ACHIEVED set. Shape D enumerates the expected
set — it just enumerates it *somewhere nothing lives*.

### Instance 5 — `origin-freshness-watchdog` swept the wrong workspace (WI-5791)

The watchdog resolved its own scope as:

```ts
const workspaceId = opts.workspaceId ?? DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID;
const projects = (await loadHarnessRegistry(workspaceId)).projects;
```

No caller has ever passed `opts.workspaceId` — the boot path is
`startOriginFreshnessWatchdog(sql)`, which forwards empty opts. And
`DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID` is the literal `'default'`: on this install a scratch
workspace holding 14 unrelated pots and **zero** bridged hives. Every real pot
lives in `'papercusp-workspace'`.

So every sweep since the watchdog shipped returned `checked: 0`. It never
entered the per-entry body, never wrote `of_origin_sha`, never aged a tip, and
therefore could never fire `tipAgeStale`. Measured, not inferred: a
write-intercepting `sql` proxy over the real registry returned
`{checked: 0, writes: 0}`, and `of_origin_sha` was NULL on all 21 `system:git-sync`
routine rows fleet-wide — every pot, not just the one under investigation.

The watchdog built to catch a silently-stalled egress was itself silently
stalled for its entire life. It was written *in response to* a five-day egress
outage, and it would not have caught that outage.

**Why nothing noticed.** `{alarmed: [], recovered: [], checked: 0}` is
success-shaped. There is no error, no throw, no warning — and no surface read
`checked`. "Covered everything, all healthy" and "covered nothing" were the same
value.

**Why the tests didn't notice.** `origin-freshness.test.ts` covered the pure
verdict functions (`evaluateOriginFreshness`, `selectOriginWatermark`)
thoroughly, and was green the whole time. `checkOriginFreshness` — the wiring
that decides *what gets judged* — had no test at all. A well-tested predicate
over an untested selection. Unit tests structurally cannot catch this, because a
test always injects an explicit `workspaceId`: the path under test is never the
production path.

**It is a class, not an instance.** At least four occurrences of
`?? DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID` silently scoping work to the wrong or empty workspace:
this one; EI-10103 (the sibling main-behind watchdog, whose escalation INSERT
then violated a NOT NULL constraint and was swallowed by its own outer catch);
an in-code comment at `agent-tools/plans/revisions.ts` recording that it read the
wrong workspace's plan spine; and `host-bootstrap`'s stall-waker looping only the
registry's first entry and no-op'ing the other 16. Tracked as
EI-18660454282479136.

### The fix shape

1. **Enumerate the scope, don't default it.** `listRegistryWorkspaceIds(sql)`
   over `harness_shared.harness_registry`, sweeping all of them.
2. **Do not fall back to the default on a failed enumeration.** That fallback
   *is* the bug. Return empty and let the guard below report it.
3. **Self-report zero coverage.** Ask a cheap, INDEPENDENT question — "were there
   bridged pots that a covering sweep must have checked?" — and if the answer is
   yes while `checked === 0`, set `blind: true` and say so at the same volume as
   a real alarm. The guard has to come from a different source than the sweep,
   or it inherits the same blindness.

The general form of (3): **any sweeper that can legitimately process zero units
needs a second, independent opinion about whether zero was the right answer.**

## Shape E — the detector switched off by the aggregate's health

Checklist question 4 below already states the rule in its "contaminated signal"
form: a signal kept fresh by something *other* than the mechanism you are
watching cannot tell you about that mechanism. This shape is its nastier
variant — the aggregate does not merely *contaminate* the detector's input, it
**gates whether the detector runs at all**.

### Instance 6 — the live-federation gate's `local-matrix` leg (EI-18657324526667507)

`live-federation-gate.sh` has a `check_staleness()` that files a loud EI when no
GREEN run has happened in `GATE_STALE_DAYS`. It opens with an early return while
the gate-wide `last-green` is fresh — reasonable in isolation.

But the gate is several legs, and the *cheap* `content-matrix` leg keeps
`last-green` fresh on its own. The heavy `local-matrix` leg had three independent
suppression paths (a `LOAD_GATE` defer, the `MATRIX_TTL_H` 144h cadence window,
and a rig-busy pre-check) that each **exit 0**. So the leg could stop deciding
anything, indefinitely, and the one detector that might have said so was
*switched off by the sibling leg's success*. Measured live: `last-matrix-green`
ABSENT — the leg had never once produced a verdict — while `last-run` was minutes
old and 205 skip banks had accumulated. A verification waiting on it stalled for
days behind an all-green gate.

Note the asymmetry that makes this hard to see in review: the detector was
correct on every RED path (it is called from all of them) and blind on exactly
the GREEN one — the state nobody investigates.

### The fix shape

1. **Give the unit its own clock.** A `last-matrix-verdict` stamp — "when did
   this leg last DECIDE anything" — kept deliberately separate from
   `last-matrix-green` ("when was it last GOOD"). They differ in both directions:
   a leg that only ever FAILs is still *running*, and a leg green last week but
   suppressed ever since is stale. Do not reuse the success stamp as the liveness
   stamp.
2. **Only a real verdict clears it.** A downgrade that means "nothing was proven"
   (here `SKIPPED-STARVATION`) must NOT stamp the clock, and a green *aggregate*
   must not clear the unit's dedup file. Otherwise the aggregate re-acquires the
   power to silence the unit.
3. **Call it on the healthy path too — that is the load-bearing call.** Wiring it
   into the paths that already report is free but proves nothing; the GREEN exit
   is the one that was hiding the failure.
4. **Derive the threshold from the cadence it watches.** `MATRIX_STALE_H =
   MATRIX_TTL_H + grace`, not a second independent constant — otherwise raising
   the cadence silently disarms its own detector, which is the same drift this
   doc's Shape A warns about one level up.

General form: **a detector scoped to an aggregate cannot report a unit inside it
going dark.** Any unit with its own suppression paths needs its own liveness
clock, checked on the aggregate's success path.

## The checklist

When you write or review a guard, latch, watchdog, or watermark:

1. **Can this state advance without the success it gates?** If no, the first
   failure is permanent. Split the work, or add a path that advances on partial
   progress.
2. **Is the clear reachable from every path?** Check reset, and every early
   `continue` / `return` before it.
3. **Does the thing being watched report its own health?** If so, consume that
   report — do not infer it.
4. **Is the signal you measure kept fresh by anything OTHER than the mechanism
   you are watching?** If yes, it cannot tell you about that mechanism. And its
   sharper form (Shape E): does that signal *gate whether your detector runs at
   all*? A detector scoped to an aggregate goes blind to any unit inside it that
   stops running while a sibling keeps the aggregate healthy.
5. **Does the escape hatch cover every instance of the guard?** An escape hatch
   present on two of three guards is absent from the one that wedges.
6. **Does the detector enumerate the EXPECTED set or the ACHIEVED set?** If it
   iterates things that already succeeded, it is structurally blind to total
   failure — the case you most need it for.
7. **Is the set it enumerates actually non-empty in production?** A correct
   enumeration pointed at the wrong scope reports a clean pass forever. If a
   zero-unit pass is possible, get a SECOND, independent opinion on whether zero
   was right — and make a wrong zero as loud as an alarm.

**Question 6 is the highest-yield of the six.** State it as a test you can apply
without reading the implementation:

> **"If this never worked even once, would this detector produce a single line?"**

If the answer is no, the detector cannot detect its own primary failure mode.

That one question catches instances 3 and 4 directly. It also catches the
`origin-freshness-watchdog` early-`continue` in Shape A above — a pot that lost
its bare store was dropped from the enumerated set entirely, which is the same
blindness arriving by a different route.

**Question 7 has its own version of that test**, and it is the one that catches
Shape D:

> **"If this detector were pointed at nothing at all, would its output differ
> from a clean pass?"**

For instance 5 the answer was no, for the entire life of the watchdog. Note that
question 6's test does NOT catch it: if origin-freshness "never worked even
once" it would still have produced a line — for a pot in the wrong workspace.
The enumeration was the right shape, aimed at an empty room.

## Provenance

Four instances, four agents, four lanes, one day:

| # | Instance | Shape | Found by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | pot-git publish guards (×3) | A | su-a8ea9 |
| 2 | replication-liveness alarm latch | A (reset path) | su-e3b21 |
| 3 | `restart_settle_barrier` (EI-18645423267952485) | C | su-48ed7a |
| 4 | replication-liveness call site (WI-5781) | C | su-055ae |
| 5 | `origin-freshness-watchdog` swept workspace `'default'` (WI-5791) | D | su-a8ea9 |

Shape B and the `origin-freshness-watchdog` latch leak: su-a8ea9.

Shape D was added the day after, from WI-5791 — which is the sharpest evidence
for this whole doc's thesis. WI-5791 was filed as a cautious follow-up to the
Shape A/B fixes, with an explicit note not to assume the benign explanation. The
benign explanation was wrong: the watchdog those fixes had just hardened had
never once looked at a real pot. Every repair in Shape A and Shape B above was
made to a detector that was, at that moment, still pointed at an empty room —
and nothing in the fix-and-verify loop surfaced that, because a zero-coverage
pass is success-shaped.

None of this was written by one agent. The general statement came out of a
coordination exchange: su-e3b21 asked whether the **reset path** had been
checked, which is the only reason the `origin-freshness-watchdog` latch leak was
found; su-e3b21 then rejected the first draft's two-instance framing, supplied
instances 3 and 4, and argued Shape C and checklist question 6 into existence —
including the observation that the *detector* failures, not the guard failures,
are the real headline. The run evidence for instance 4 is su-055ae's.
